The ancient Romans were known for their outstanding engineering skills, and the streets of Pompeii are no exception. These streets are a time capsule of Roman history, architecture and engineering. They offer us a(n) [[1]] into the daily lives of the citizens of Pompeii and how they traveled through their town.
The cobblestones, which were made from large blocks of lava from Mt Vesuvius, are one of the most significant features of Pompeii’s streets. These stones were perfectly fitted together, [[2]] expert skills of the Romans. Most streets were not wider than 4.5 meters and were limited to one-way traffic. As you can see from the wheel tracks, or “ruts,” left behind in the cobblestones, narrower streets were used mainly by chariots and carts. These carts were used to transport goods, food and other materials, and their wheels were rimmed with iron. Iron stains left by the wheels are still [[3]] on some street tracks. These tracks were up to 6 inches deep, making a clear wear pattern on the ground.
Pompeii had no sewage system or drainage system, so waste and mud built up in the streets. The streets were lined with houses and shops, and wastewater and trash were also [[4]] there. As you walk down these streets, you’ll notice “crosswalks” made of massive stone pieces that are the same [[5]] as the sidewalks. These were designed to allow people to cross the street without touching the organic waste, water, and garbage in the streets. The crosswalks were [[6]] positioned, with spaces in between for carts to pass through. They are thought to be the first pedestrian crossings in history.
The streets themselves were [[7]] higher in the center to allow waste and water to run into the gutters along the sides. However, due to a lack of a proper drainage system, this was not always [[8]]. Sidewalk curbs were usually at least 30 centimeters higher than the streets. This [[9]] the sidewalks from street waste and ensured that the sidewalks were not affected during street cleaning. So the next time you visit the [[10]] of Pompeii, be sure to take a closer look at its streets. You will be amazed at the creative thinking of the ancient Romans.
